title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Darya Alexandrovna spent the summer with her children at Pokrovskoe, at her sister Kitty Levin's. Her own estate was practically a ruin, and the Levins had pressed her to spend the season with them. Stepan Arkadyevitch heartily approved. He kept saying how sorry he was that his official duties kept him from spending the whole summer in the country with his family — which would have been his greatest happiness — and so he stayed in Moscow and came down for a day or two now and then. Beyond the Oblonskys, with all their children and their governess, the old princess had also come for the summer; she felt it her duty to keep an eye on her inexperienced daughter in her _interesting condition_. On top of that, Varenka, Kitty's friend from abroad, had kept her promise to visit Kitty once she was married and had come to stay. Every one of these guests was a friend or relative of Levin's wife. He liked them all, but he still missed his own Levin world and Levin ways, which were being smothered under this incoming tide of what he privately called the "Shtcherbatsky element." Of his own relations, only Sergey Ivanovitch was staying with him, and even he was cast in the Koznishev rather than the Levin mold, so that the Levin spirit had been thoroughly drowned out.

The Levins' house, empty for so long, was now so full that nearly every room was occupied, and almost every day, sitting down at table, the old princess counted heads and had to set the thirteenth grandchild at a separate table. And Kitty, careful housekeeper that she was, had no small trouble keeping the place supplied with chickens, turkeys, and geese — so many were needed to satisfy the summer appetites of guests and children.

The whole family was at dinner. Dolly's children, along with their governess and Varenka, were planning a mushroom-hunting expedition. Sergey Ivanovitch, whom the rest of the company regarded with a near-reverence for his intellect and learning, startled everyone by joining the mushroom conversation.
"Take me along. I'm very fond of mushroom-picking," he said, looking at Varenka. "It strikes me as a delightful pastime."

"We'd be glad to have you," Varenka answered, coloring slightly. Kitty and Dolly traded a meaningful glance. The fact that the learned, intellectual Sergey Ivanovitch wanted to go mushroom-picking with Varenka confirmed certain theories of Kitty's that her mind had been chewing on lately. She hurried to say something to her mother so that nobody would catch the look. After dinner Sergey Ivanovitch took his coffee to the drawing-room window, and while he carried on a conversation with his brother he kept an eye on the door through which the children would head out for their expedition. Levin sat at the next window beside him.
Kitty stood next to her husband, clearly waiting for the end of a conversation that did not interest her so that she could tell him something.

"You've changed in many ways since you married, and all for the better," Sergey Ivanovitch said with a smile to Kitty, plainly not very absorbed in the talk, "but you've kept that loyalty of yours to the most paradoxical theories."
"Katya, it isn't good for you to stand," her husband told her, setting a chair for her and giving her a meaningful look.
"And there's no time anyway," Sergey Ivanovitch added, seeing the children come running.
At the head of them all came Tanya, her stockings drawn tight, galloping sideways with a basket in one hand and Sergey Ivanovitch's hat in the other. She ran straight up to him.
Walking boldly up to Sergey Ivanovitch with shining eyes — so like her father's fine eyes — she handed him his hat and made as if to put it on for him, softening her cheek with a shy, friendly smile.
"Varenka's waiting," she said, carefully fitting the hat on, gathering from Sergey Ivanovitch's smile that she had permission to.
Varenka was standing in the doorway in a yellow print dress with a white kerchief on her head.
"Coming, coming, Varvara Andreevna," said Sergey Ivanovitch, finishing his cup of coffee and tucking his handkerchief and cigar-case into separate pockets.

"Isn't my Varenka sweet? Well?" Kitty said to her husband the moment Sergey Ivanovitch stood up. She pitched her voice so that Sergey Ivanovitch would hear, and meant him to. "And how good-looking — such a refined beauty! Varenka!" Kitty called out. "Will you be in the mill copse? We'll come out and meet you there."
"You really do forget your condition, Kitty," said the old princess, hurrying out through the door. "You mustn't shout like that."

Hearing Kitty's voice and her mother's scolding, Varenka came over to Kitty with quick, light steps. The rapidity of her movement, her flushed and eager face — everything betrayed that something out of the ordinary was happening in her. Kitty knew what it was; she had been watching her closely. She had called Varenka over now only to give her, silently, a blessing for the great event which, as Kitty imagined it, was bound to happen that day after dinner in the wood.
"Varenka, I'd be very happy if a certain something were to happen," she whispered as she kissed her.
"And are you coming with us?" Varenka said to Levin in confusion, pretending she had not heard what had been said.
"I'm coming, but only as far as the threshing-floor — I'll stop there."
"What do you want there?" Kitty asked.
"I have to take a look at the new wagons, and check the invoice," Levin said. "And where will you be?"
"On the terrace."
